concepts.maxim: Treat others as you would wish to be treated.
concepts.summary: Perhaps the most widely shared rule for living. Long before these traditions could read one another, each arrived at the same quiet test: before you act, put yourself in the other person's place.

concepts.maxim: Life contains suffering; begin by accepting it.
concepts.summary: Not a counsel of despair, but a starting point. Naming the hardness of life honestly frees us to respond to it with courage rather than surprise.

concepts.maxim: Craving is the root of suffering.
concepts.summary: Much of our pain comes not from what happens, but from our grasping for things to be otherwise. Loosen the grip and the weight lightens.

concepts.maxim: Be present: the here and now is where life happens.
concepts.summary: The past has gone and the future has not arrived. The present moment is the only place we can actually live, act and enjoy.

concepts.maxim: Treat yourself like someone you are responsible for helping.
concepts.summary: We often care better for others than for ourselves. Extend the same kindness and discipline inward.

concepts.maxim: Find meaning in the struggle itself.
concepts.summary: Sisyphus pushes his boulder up the hill forever. The ancient myth was a punishment; the modern reading asks whether the effort itself can be enough.

concepts.maxim: Leave things better than you found them.
concepts.summary: A simple measure for a day, a campsite or a life: did the world come out a little ahead for your having passed through?

concepts.maxim: Keep it simple.
concepts.summary: Complexity is costly and fragile. The simplest design that works is usually the one that lasts.

concepts.maxim: A few causes drive most results (the 80/20 rule).
concepts.summary: Effort and outcome are rarely in proportion. Find the vital few things that matter and give them your best attention.
concepts.hold: The older quotes here (Marcus Aurelius, Luke 10) echo only the 'focus on what matters' half of this idea, not the claim that a few causes drive most results, so it waits in Emerging until a closer independent source is found.

concepts.maxim: People rise to their level of incompetence.
concepts.summary: A gently humbling observation about organisations: we tend to be promoted until we land in a role we no longer do well. Know your strengths.

concepts.maxim: Happiness is reality minus expectations.
concepts.summary: A popular modern formula. When expectations outrun reality, disappointment fills the gap; holding them lightly leaves room for contentment.

concepts.maxim: Do your work wholeheartedly and with skill.
concepts.summary: Whatever is in front of you, give it your full strength. Skill grows quietly out of repeated, careful effort, and in time it opens doors.

concepts.maxim: Pursue what is meaningful, not what is merely profitable.
concepts.summary: Chase the thing that matters to you rather than the quick reward. A life built around meaning tends to carry its own momentum.

concepts.maxim: Ability grows with effort; measure yourself against who you were yesterday.
concepts.summary: Talents are a starting point, not a verdict. The useful comparison is with your own past self, and every honest effort moves the line.

concepts.maxim: More choice does not always mean more happiness.
concepts.summary: An endless menu can leave us anxious and second-guessing. Sometimes choosing 'good enough' and letting go is the wiser path.

concepts.maxim: There is a time for everything; give your days a rhythm.
concepts.summary: Life moves in seasons and cycles. A steady rhythm of rising, working, eating and resting makes room for everything else.

concepts.maxim: Tell the truth, or at least don't lie.
concepts.summary: Honesty keeps our footing sure. Each small truth makes the world, and ourselves, a little easier to trust.

concepts.maxim: Your thoughts shape your life.
concepts.summary: What we dwell on becomes the lens we see through, and then the ground we stand on. Tending the mind is tending the life.

concepts.maxim: Seek the middle way; avoid extremes.
concepts.summary: Too much and too little both lead us astray. Again and again the old teachers point to a balanced path between the extremes, harder to find than either, but steadier to walk.

concepts.maxim: Meet hatred with love and evil with good.
concepts.summary: Answering harm with harm only keeps the wheel turning. Many traditions ask something harder and braver: to break the cycle by returning kindness, even to an enemy.

concepts.maxim: Know yourself.
concepts.summary: Understanding the world begins close to home. To look honestly at our own motives, limits and ignorance is a lifelong task, and perhaps the beginning of every other kind of wisdom.

concepts.maxim: Be humble; pride goes before a fall.
concepts.summary: Those who lift themselves up tend to be brought low, while those who hold themselves lightly are trusted and remembered. Humility is not thinking less of ourselves, but seeing ourselves truly.

concepts.maxim: Be slow to anger; master yourself.
concepts.summary: Anger arrives quickly and leaves damage behind it. Real strength, these voices agree, lies less in overpowering others than in holding the reins of our own temper.

concepts.maxim: Remember that you will die, and live well today.
concepts.summary: Our days are numbered, and remembering it is not morbid but clarifying. Keeping death in view shrinks petty quarrels and turns us back towards what is good while we still can.

concepts.maxim: Speak kindly, or keep silent.
concepts.summary: Words can heal or wound, and once spoken they cannot be taken back. A little restraint in speech spares others pain and spares us a good deal of trouble.

concepts.maxim: Give thanks.
concepts.summary: Gratitude turns what we have into enough, and it notices the kindness we would otherwise take for granted. Saying thank you, to people and to life, softens the heart and makes room for joy.

concepts.maxim: Forgive, and keep forgiving.
concepts.summary: Everyone stumbles, and everyone needs pardon at some point. Letting go of a grievance frees the one who forgives as much as the one forgiven.

concepts.maxim: Give freely; generosity enriches the giver.
concepts.summary: What we give away has a strange way of coming back as a fuller life. An open hand makes room for connection, and it loosens the grip that possessions can have on us.

concepts.maxim: Everything passes; hold things lightly.
concepts.summary: Nothing we see stays the same, not our troubles, our triumphs or the world around us. Remembering this can steady us in hard times and keep us gentle in good ones.

concepts.maxim: Do what is right, even when you are afraid.
concepts.summary: Courage is not the absence of fear but the choice to act well in its presence. Most of the good we do asks a little bravery of us.

concepts.maxim: Be patient; endure, and let things ripen.
concepts.summary: Much of what matters grows slowly and cannot be hurried. Patience is the quiet strength that holds steady through difficulty and waits for the right moment.

concepts.maxim: Great things begin with small steps.
concepts.summary: Every large work starts as something tiny and easy to overlook. Taking the next small step, and being faithful in little things, is how anything worthwhile gets built.

concepts.maxim: Look to your own faults before judging others.
concepts.summary: It is easy to see what others get wrong and hard to see our own failings. Turning the light on ourselves first makes us both wiser and kinder.

concepts.maxim: Choose your companions wisely.
concepts.summary: We slowly become like the people we spend our days with. Seeking out good, honest friends is one of the surest ways to grow into a better person.

concepts.maxim: Welcome the stranger.
concepts.summary: Almost every tradition treats the guest and the traveller as someone to honour. Opening our door, and our table, reminds us that we too have been strangers somewhere.

concepts.maxim: Honour your father and your mother.
concepts.summary: The people who raised us gave us our first world, however imperfectly. Many traditions ask us to meet them with care and respect, not just duty, and to let that gratitude show in how we treat them as they grow older.

concepts.maxim: Let your actions match your words.
concepts.summary: Fine words cost little; what we do shows what we really believe. Living out what we say, quietly and first, is how trust is built, in others and in ourselves.

concepts.maxim: Keep learning, all your life.
concepts.summary: Learning is not a stage we finish but a way of staying awake to the world. Traditions far apart describe it as a quiet pleasure, the mark of someone wise enough to know there is always more to hear.

concepts.maxim: Listen more than you speak.
concepts.summary: Real listening is a kind of generosity, and a kind of humility too. When we assume the other person may know something we don't, conversations stop being contests and start teaching us.

concepts.maxim: Do what is just, even when it costs you.
concepts.summary: Justice asks us to be fair when fairness is inconvenient: to our rivals, to strangers, and against our own interest. Many traditions hold that it is better to suffer a wrong than to do one, and that a fair heart is worth more than any advantage.

concepts.maxim: Be merciful to every living being.
concepts.summary: Mercy is kindness offered where it was not earned. Traditions across the world ask us to widen our care, from family to stranger to every creature that breathes, and find that a softer heart is also a freer one.

concepts.maxim: Seek peace, and pursue it.
concepts.summary: Peace rarely arrives by itself; it is something we go after, in quarrels at home as much as between nations. To be the one who lowers the temperature, and who takes the offered hand, is honoured in nearly every tradition.

concepts.maxim: First, do no harm.
concepts.summary: Before we try to help, we can at least refuse to hurt. This simple restraint, shared by healers, monks and moralists, asks us to remember that every living being, like us, fears pain and loves life.

concepts.maxim: Keep your promises; let your yes mean yes.
concepts.summary: A promise is a small piece of the future we give to someone else. Keeping it, or not making it lightly, is how trust grows, and how our words come to carry weight.

concepts.maxim: Make time for stillness.
concepts.summary: Much of our restlessness comes from never stopping. Contemplatives, philosophers and psalmists alike point to a quiet place within, always available, where we can rest, see clearly and return refreshed.

concepts.maxim: Admit your mistakes and put them right.
concepts.summary: Everyone falls short; what matters is what we do next. Owning a fault, rather than hiding it, is the first step to mending it, and a mended fault can leave us brighter than before.

concepts.maxim: When you fall, get back up.
concepts.summary: Falling is not the failure; staying down is. Traditions far apart in time and place honour the person who stumbles, gathers themselves, and rises again, as many times as it takes.

quotes.work: 12 Rules for Life (2018), Rule 9 (rule title); checked via Wikipedia, not the book

quotes.text: That which is altogether just shalt thou follow, that thou mayest live, and inherit the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee.
He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
O ye who believe! stand fast to justice, when ye bear witness before God, though it be against yourselves, or your parents, or your kindred, whether the party be rich or poor.
quotes.work: Qur'an 4:135 (Sura An-Nisa, 'Women'), tr. J. M. Rodwell

quotes.text: I should not like either, but if I must choose between them, I would rather suffer than do.
quotes.work: Plato, Gorgias 469c, tr. Benjamin Jowett; Socrates on whether he would rather suffer or do injustice

quotes.text: Even as a mother protects with her life Her child, her only child, So with a boundless heart Should one cherish all living beings;
quotes.work: Karaniya Metta Sutta (Sn 1.8), tr. the Amaravati Sangha

quotes.text: Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful.
Allah will not be merciful to those who are not merciful to mankind.
quotes.thinker: The Prophet Muhammad (narrated by Jarir bin Abdullah)
quotes.translation: Muhsin Khan translation, as given on sunnah.com

quotes.text: The merciful are shown mercy by Ar-Rahman. Be merciful on the earth, and you will be shown mercy from Who is above the heavens.
quotes.thinker: The Prophet Muhammad (narrated by Abdullah bin 'Amr)
quotes.work: Jami` at-Tirmidhi 1924 (graded hasan sahih by at-Tirmidhi)
quotes.translation: English translation as given on sunnah.com

quotes.text: Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding.
Learning without thought is labour lost; thought without learning is perilous.
Seeking knowledge is a duty upon every Muslim,
quotes.thinker: The Prophet Muhammad (narrated by Anas bin Malik)
quotes.work: Sunan Ibn Majah 224; sunnah.com notes this opening phrase is authentic through many routes, the rest of the narration is weak and is not quoted
quotes.translation: English translation as given on sunnah.com

quotes.text: Depart from evil, and do good; seek peace, and pursue it.
be of the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace, loving mankind and drawing them close to the Torah.
quotes.work: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 1:12, tr. Joshua Kulp (Mishnah Yomit)
quotes.translation: Sefaria / Mishnah Yomit by Dr. Joshua Kulp (CC BY)

quotes.text: Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.
And if they lean to peace, lean thou also to it; and put thy trust in God: for He is the Hearing, the Knowing.
quotes.work: Qur'an 8:61 (Sura Al-Anfal, 'The Spoils'), tr. J. M. Rodwell

quotes.text: Victory breeds hatred, for the conquered is unhappy. He who has given up both victory and defeat, he, the contented, is happy.
Calm and repose are what he prizes; victory (by force of arms) is to him undesirable.
quotes.work: Tao Te Ching, ch. 31, tr. James Legge

quotes.text: have two special objects in view with regard to diseases, namely, to do good or to do no harm.
quotes.work: Epidemics, Book I, section 2, tr. Francis Adams (The Genuine Works of Hippocrates, 1849)

quotes.text: all breathing, existing, living, sentient creatures should not be slain, nor treated with violence, nor abused, nor tormented, nor driven away.
quotes.work: Acaranga Sutra, Book I, Lecture 4, Lesson 1, tr. Hermann Jacobi (Sacred Books of the East 22)

quotes.text: All men tremble at punishment, all men fear death; remember that you are like unto them, and do not kill, nor cause slaughter.
Love worketh no ill to his neighbour: therefore love is the fulfilling of the law.
Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay.
But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.
And perform your covenant; verily the covenant shall be enquired of:
quotes.work: Qur'an 17:34 (Sura Al-Isra, 'The Night Journey'), tr. J. M. Rodwell

quotes.text: I do not know how a man without truthfulness is to get on.
quotes.work: Analects 2.22, tr. James Legge (the word rendered "truthfulness", xin, also means keeping faith)

quotes.text: The (state of) vacancy should be brought to the utmost degree, and that of stillness guarded with unwearying vigour.
quotes.work: Tao Te Ching, ch. 16, tr. James Legge

quotes.text: it is in thy power whenever thou shalt choose to retire into thyself. For nowhere either with more quiet or more freedom from trouble does a man retire than into his own soul,
quotes.work: Meditations, Book IV.3, tr. George Long

quotes.text: I have discovered that all the unhappiness of men arises from one single fact, that they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber.
quotes.work: Pensées, no. 139, tr. W. F. Trotter

quotes.text: Be still, and know that I am God:
quotes.work: Psalm 46:10 (KJV); stillness here is in the presence of God

quotes.text: Thy Lord hath ordained that ye worship none but him; and, kindness to your parents, whether one or both of them attain to old age with thee: and say not to them, "Fie!" neither reproach them; but speak to them both with respectful speech;
quotes.work: Qur'an 17:23 (Sura Al-Isra, 'The Night Journey'), tr. J. M. Rodwell

quotes.text: Believers! why profess ye that which ye practise not? Most hateful is it to God that ye say that which ye do not.
quotes.work: Qur'an 61:2–3 (Sura As-Saff, 'Battle Array'), tr. J. M. Rodwell

quotes.text: Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them.
Order. Let all your things have their places; let each part of your business have its time.
Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the desire: this is also vanity and vexation of spirit.
He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him.
That man himself found a world full of carob trees. Just as my ancestors planted for me, I too am planting for my descendants.
quotes.thinker: Anonymous (the carob planter, told of Honi HaMe'aggel)
quotes.work: Babylonian Talmud, Taanit 23a, William Davidson Edition (Koren-Steinsaltz)
quotes.translation: William Davidson Edition English translation, CC BY-NC (via Sefaria)

quotes.text: we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope:
But simple views, and courses plain and true Would selfish ends and many lusts eschew.
quotes.work: Tao Te Ching, ch. 19, tr. James Legge (Legge's verse rendering)

quotes.text: Simplicity is the ultimate sophistication.
quotes.thinker: Unknown (often misattributed to Leonardo da Vinci)
quotes.work: Popular attribution to Leonardo; Quote Investigator finds no evidence he said it (earliest Leonardo attribution c. 2000). Closest early match: Clare Boothe Luce, Stuffed Shirts (1931): "the height of sophistication is simplicity."

quotes.text: A man should say, I am not concerned that I have no place, I am concerned how I may fit myself for one.
If you can one day renovate yourself, do so from day to day. Yea, let there be daily renovation.
quotes.thinker: The Great Learning (inscription of King Tang)
quotes.work: The Great Learning (Daxue), commentary ch. 2, tr. James Legge

quotes.text: To have faults and not to reform them,-- this, indeed, should be pronounced having faults.
He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy.
He whose evil deeds are covered by good deeds, brightens up this world, like the moon when freed from clouds.
For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again: but the wicked shall fall into mischief.
Our greatest glory is, not in never falling; but in rising every time we fall.
quotes.work: The Citizen of the World (1762), vol. 1, Letter VII. Spoken by Goldsmith's fictional Chinese narrator, who credits Confucius; the line is not found in Confucius's works (see Quote Investigator, https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/05/27/rising/). Spelling modernised from the long s.
